vignette:
He is a 74-year-old European man who comes across as thoughtful and composed at first, with the careful, measured way of someone who has spent much of his life helping others make sense of difficult things. He works as a tutor, and until recently that role gave shape to his days. He likes the rhythm of teaching one person at a time, the sense that he can still be useful, still steady, still able to guide someone through confusion. He lives with a partner, and he speaks of the relationship with warmth, though it is clear that lately he has been more withdrawn than he wants to admit.

The disaster happens two years ago, in the middle of the night, when heavy rain turns to flooding with alarming speed. He is woken by a pounding noise he initially cannot place, then by the realization that water is entering the home. He describes the scene with a kind of disbelief that never fully left him: the dark house, the sound of rushing water outside, his partner’s voice strained with fear, the scramble to gather documents, medication, and a few treasured photographs before the power fails. He remembers the coldness of the water rising around his ankles, then his knees, and the strange, humiliating helplessness of being unable to stop what is happening. What stays with him most is not only the danger but the speed of it. He had always thought of himself as practical, someone who could respond calmly in a crisis, yet in that moment his mind goes blank. He says he keeps seeing the look on his partner’s face when she realizes they may not be able to save everything.

In the weeks after, he functions more than he feels. He helps with cleanup, makes endless phone calls to insurance, catalogues losses, and tries to reassure others. He tells friends that they were lucky, because they survived. He repeats this often, almost as if he is trying to convince himself. But once the immediate urgency passes, he notices that he cannot settle. Sleep becomes broken and shallow. He wakes before dawn with his heart racing, listening for sounds that are not there. When it rains, even lightly, his body tightens before he is aware of it. He finds himself checking weather reports several times a day, studying clouds, watching drains, scanning roads for water. He begins to avoid driving near the river and refuses invitations from acquaintances who have moved back into flood-prone areas. He says he used to enjoy long walks after dinner, but now he prefers to stay close to home, especially in the evening when shadows gather and the world feels less predictable.

As a tutor, he notices the changes in his concentration most sharply when he is trying to prepare lessons. He reads the same page repeatedly and realizes he has not taken in a word. In sessions with students, he occasionally loses his thread, something he finds embarrassing because he has always prided himself on being attentive and articulate. He worries that age is catching up with him, though he also knows this is different; it feels like his mind keeps slipping away to the night of the flood without warning. A sound outside the window, the smell of damp earth, or a sudden weather alert on the radio can pull him back so vividly that he is no longer entirely in the present. When this happens, he becomes quiet and distant. His partner notices that he sometimes stands in doorways, staring, as if he has gone somewhere else.

He does not speak easily about fear. Instead, he describes a persistent unease, a sense that the world has become less reliable. He feels irritated by small disruptions, then ashamed of his impatience. He is more cautious with money, more controlling about household preparations, and more reluctant to let go of plans. At times he feels an unexpected wave of sadness over what was lost: not only possessions, but the easy confidence he once had in ordinary safety. He misses the version of himself who could absorb difficulty without becoming preoccupied by it.

Still, there are moments when he tries to reach outward again. He returns to tutoring because it gives him structure and because young people, he says, keep him from sinking too far into his own thoughts. He notices that teaching helps for a while; explaining a problem to a student can draw him back into the room. But even there he remains vigilant, listening for weather on the roof, glancing toward windows when the sky darkens. He lives now in the shadow of that night, not constantly, but often enough that his days are organized around avoiding surprise.
